Sunday lunch
Mum burnt the dodo again but nobody said anything because she'd been up since 6 making stew. Uncle Femi ate four pieces anyway.
Dad carved the chicken while my aunt argued about the football. Someone dropped a spoon, the dog got a roast potato, and we were still at the table at four.
A rainy commute
Bus didn't come for 25 mins, then two came at once. Got soaked walking from the stop and my left sock is still wet.
The 8:15 was cancelled, so I stood under the shelter with six strangers and one umbrella between us.
First flat
Our first flat had a boiler that only worked if you kicked it. We called it Bola. We still talk about Bola.
Our first flat had one working socket and a window that wouldn't close. We ate noodles on the floor for a month and thought it was the best place ever.
Airport delay
Flight pushed back 3 hours. Ate a £9 sandwich, charged my phone on the floor next to a man asleep on his suitcase.
Our gate changed twice and the board kept saying 'delayed' with no reason.
Birthday cake
Sister forgot the candles so we stuck a sparkler in it. Smoke alarm went off. Best birthday honestly.
Mum ordered a lemon cake but the shop wrote the wrong name on it. We kept it anyway and he spent the evening answering to 'Dave'.
The group chat
My cousins' group chat is 90% voice notes and one guy who only replies with a thumbs up. Nobody has ever left.
The family group chat has three rules: no politics, no spoilers, and everyone must reply to birthday messages within the hour. Only the last one is enforced.
Gym in January
Gym was rammed on the 2nd. By the 20th I had my pick of treadmills again. I'm not judging, I was in the crowd.
The gym was full on the second of January and half empty by the end of the month. I stayed on the same machine, mostly out of stubbornness.
Lost keys
Spent 20 minutes turning the flat upside down for my keys. They were in the door. On the outside. All night.
I searched the coat pockets, the sofa and the bin before finding the keys in the fridge next to the milk.
Late night shop
Corner shop guy knows my order now. Two bananas, a Twix, whatever's left of the bread. He just nods.
The man at the corner shop remembers that I buy oat milk on Thursdays and says nothing about it. I like how he understands without asking.
Moving house
Third box I opened was just cables. Nobody knows what they connect to. We're keeping them anyway.
The removal van arrived early, so I was still in pyjamas holding a kettle.
Wedding speech
My brother's best man speech had a slide of his ex. Nobody breathed. Then the bride laughed and everyone relaxed.
The best man spoke for twelve minutes, mostly about a camping trip. He forgot the groom's surname once and recovered by pretending it was a joke.
Street food
Jollof from the van near the station, paid cash, sat on a wall. Burnt my tongue on the first bite, no regrets.
The stall by the station sells suya wrapped in paper, and the queue moves fast.
Bad haircut
Asked for a trim, got a fade I did not request. Wore a hat for a week, then it grew out and I'm fine.
The barber was chatting about the cricket and kept cutting. By the time I looked up, my fringe had gone. It grew back, and I learned to watch the mirror.
Charity run
Did the 5k for charity. Walked the last bit, got a banana and a medal that is clearly plastic. Proud of it.
I signed up for the 5k on a whim and trained for two weeks.
Phone battery
Phone died at 4% on the way home, so I navigated by vibes and a vague memory of the bus route. Got there eventually.
My phone shut down halfway through the journey, so I asked a stranger for directions and ended up in a ten-minute conversation about her allotment.
School reunion
Went to the reunion expecting to feel old. Mostly felt relieved nobody remembered the thing with the fire extinguisher.
At the reunion everyone had less hair and better stories. The quiet boy from the back row now runs a bakery, and he brought the cake.
Night shift
Finished at 7am, got on a bus full of people just starting their day. Felt like I was in a different timezone to everyone.
Finished at seven, walked out into the morning rush with my lanyard still on.
Cooking for in-laws
Made egusi for the first time for her parents. Too much salt but her dad had seconds, so either it was good or he's polite.
Cooked stew for my in-laws and watched their faces for the first spoonful. Her mum said it was lovely, and I'm still trying to decode her tone.
Learning to drive
Third attempt at the test. Examiner said nothing the whole time, which felt worse than if he'd told me off. Passed, somehow.
Failed on a roundabout the first time, then passed on the second with two minors. The examiner shook my hand, which I did not expect.
New job nerves
Day one, got lost looking for the kitchen, met half the team in the stairwell. They've since decided I'm 'the lost guy'.
First day, I spent ten minutes in the wrong lift and arrived to a meeting already in progress.
Football on Saturday
Lost 4-1, still went to the pub after. Someone said 'at least we had the better kit' and honestly that's all we had.
We lost two-nil in the rain and then stood around the pub talking about next week like it was a title decider. It was the fourth division.
Quiet library
The library had a man humming the whole time and a woman who kept glaring at him. I came for peace and got a drama.
The reading room was silent except for one chair with a squeak. Every time someone shifted, the whole room looked up, then pretended it hadn't.
Grocery receipt
Went in for milk, came out with £47 of stuff and no milk. I don't know how this keeps happening.
I went in for bread and left with olives, candles and a tiny lamp. The bread was apparently sold out, or I forgot to look.
Old photographs
Found a shoebox of photos at my mum's. Me at 8 with a missing tooth, holding a fish nearly as big as me. No idea where.
Found a box of old photographs under the stairs. There was one of my dad as a teenager, grinning in a jacket three sizes too big.
Hospital waiting room
Waited 3 hours. The vending machine ate my pound. A little kid kept offering everyone his crisps, which was the best bit.
The waiting room clock was ten minutes slow, so everyone had a different idea of how long we'd been there. A child shared biscuits around.
Neighbour dispute
Neighbour's bins have been on my side for a week. I left a note. He left a longer note. We're now in a note situation.
My neighbour parks half on my drive, and I've started leaving polite notes.
Birthday voice note
Sent my brother a 4 minute birthday voice note and it got cut off mid-sentence. He replied 'love you too' anyway.
My sister sends birthday voice notes so long they need chapters. This year's had a cough, a dog, and a recipe in the middle.
Snow day
Woke up to snow, school shut, kids lost it. Spent the day sledging on a tray. Knees will recover eventually.
It snowed overnight and by eight the street was full of people in pyjamas and wellies. Someone had already made a snowman out of a bin.
Late train
Train said 12 mins late, then 25, then 'cancelled'. Everyone on the platform made eye contact like we'd survived something.
The 18:42 was cancelled, then reinstated, then cancelled again. We all drifted to the bench together like it was a support group.
First snow of winter
First snow and my coat is somehow still in the loft. Wore two jumpers and my mum's scarf. I looked like a lamp.
The first snow came before I'd dug out my gloves. I borrowed a pair from a colleague and wore them all day like a trophy.
Market stall
Sold out of plantain chips by noon, then spent the afternoon refusing to admit I'd underpriced them. Next week, £3.
The stall opened at nine and I'd sold the first batch by eleven. The woman next door told me to double the price, and she was right.
Gym buddy
My gym buddy cancels every other week. I go anyway and pretend it's his fault when I skip the heavy stuff.
My gym partner texts 'running late' and arrives forty minutes later with snacks.
Walking at dusk
There's a stretch of the canal path where the lamps come on one at a time, a little late, as if the street is clearing its throat. I walk it slower than I need to.
There is a stretch of the towpath where the lamps flicker on one by one, each a moment later than the last. I find myself walking more slowly there, in no hurry to arrive.
My grandmother's kitchen
Her kitchen smelled of onions and Dettol, and the radio was always half a station off. I never asked her why. Now I'd give a lot to hear the static.
Her kitchen smelled of onions and disinfectant, and the radio was never quite tuned. I never asked why. Now I would give a great deal to hear that static again.
Letters not sent
I wrote him a letter and never posted it. It's in a drawer with the takeaway menus and the spare keys, between the ordinary things.
I wrote him a letter and never sent it. It sits in a drawer among the takeaway menus and spare keys, an unsent thing amid the ordinary ones.
The last train
The last train was almost empty. A man was asleep with his head against the glass, and I kept my eyes on the dark so I wouldn't wake him.
The last train was nearly empty. One passenger slept against the window, and I kept watching the dark outside to avoid disturbing him.
Hospital corridor
The corridor smelled of floor polish. I counted the ceiling tiles twice, as if the number might change if I got it right.
The corridor smelled of polish and something sharper underneath. I counted the ceiling tiles, then counted them again, hoping the total would change.
Leaving home
I packed in a hurry and forgot the charger. My mother handed me hers at the door without a word, and I carried it for years.
I packed in a rush and forgot my charger. At the door, my mother placed hers in my hand, and I kept it long after it stopped working.
After the argument
We didn't speak in the car. The indicator ticked for what felt like a week, and I wondered who would break first.
We drove home in silence, the indicator ticking like a clock between us.
The empty chair
Nobody sat in his chair at the next Christmas. We laid the table around it, as one does with a thing you can't quite say.
At the next Christmas no one sat in his chair. We set the table around it carefully, the way you walk round something you cannot say aloud.
A city at six a.m.
At six the city belongs to street sweepers and bakers. I walked through it with my coat open, feeling like a guest who had arrived too early.
At six the city is all street sweepers and bakeries, and I moved through it with my coat undone, an early guest at a party not yet begun.
Old friend
We hadn't spoken in ten years, yet she picked up the conversation mid-sentence, as if I'd only gone to the kettle.
We hadn't spoken in a decade, but she continued mid-sentence, as though I had simply stepped out to make tea.
First snowfall in the city
The snow arrived overnight. By morning even the traffic had gone gentle, and a man was photographing a bin as though it were a cathedral.
Snow arrived overnight, and by morning the traffic had softened. A man was photographing a bin with great care, as though it were a cathedral.
Mother's voice
Her voice on the answerphone is still there. I don't play it, but I haven't deleted it. It's enough to know it exists.
Her voice is still on my old answerphone. I don't play it, but I haven't deleted it either. It is enough to know it is there.
Small kindness
A stranger held the door and then, noticing my shopping, held it again for my second trip. It was the smallest thing and it carried me home.
A stranger held the door open, then waited as I came back for the second bag. It was a tiny thing, yet it carried me all the way home.
The pier in winter
The pier was closed, the arcade shuttered, and gulls stood about like off-duty staff. I stayed longer than the cold advised.
In winter the pier is shuttered and the gulls loiter like staff on a break. I stayed far longer than the weather suggested.
Handwriting
Her handwriting leaned backwards, as if resisting the page. I found it on a recipe card and read it three times without cooking anything.
Her handwriting slanted backwards, as though resisting the page. I found it on a recipe card and read it again and again, never cooking a thing.
Waiting for results
I refreshed the page until my thumb ached. When it finally loaded, I closed my eyes, then felt faintly ridiculous and opened them.
I kept refreshing the page until my thumb hurt. When the result appeared, I shut my eyes, felt a little silly, and opened them again.
Barbecue
Dad guards the grill like it's a nuclear reactor. Nobody else is allowed to touch the tongs. The sausages were raw in the middle again.
Dad runs the barbecue with total authority while the rest of us hover with plates. This year the burgers were perfect, the sausages were not, and nobody said a word.
Supermarket queue
Picked the shortest queue, obviously the wrong one. Woman in front had 40 coupons and a long story about her cat.
I chose the shortest queue and it turned out to be the slowest.
Barber shop
Barber talked about his holiday in Tenerife for the whole cut. I now know more about his hotel than my own street.
My barber narrated his entire holiday while trimming my hair, down to the breakfast buffet. I nodded politely and left with a good cut and a lot of knowledge about sunbeds.
Pub quiz
We came last. Our team name was 'Quizzy Rascals'. We got the geography round right and nothing else, but the chips were good.
Our team came dead last at the pub quiz, though we did win the picture round.
Car boot sale
Went to the car boot sale for one lamp, came back with a lamp, a bread maker, and a box of VHS tapes. Nobody owns a VHS player.
At the car boot sale I haggled a man down from five pounds to four for a vase. I felt like a champion and then noticed it had a chip.
Bus driver
The driver waited while a lady ran for the bus, even though we were late. Everyone clapped when she got on. Faith in people restored.
The bus driver saw a woman sprinting down the road and waited for her, holding up the whole route. She thanked him twice, and a few passengers smiled.
Family WhatsApp
My aunt sends 'Good morning' with a glitter picture every day at 5am. Nobody replies. Nobody wants her to stop.
My aunt posts a sparkly good morning picture every day at dawn, and no one has the heart to mute her.
Camping trip
Pitched the tent in the dark, woke up on a slope. Spent the night rolling into my brother. Midges ate us alive.
We pitched the tent in the rain, discovered we'd brought the wrong poles, and spent the night under a flapping sheet. By morning we were laughing about it.
Rainy picnic
Packed a full picnic, sat in the car with the heater on and ate sandwiches watching raindrops race down the windscreen.
It started raining just as we unpacked the picnic, so we squeezed into the car with the sandwiches and a flask.
Lift small talk
Stood in a lift with my boss for twelve floors. We discussed the weather in great detail. Neither of us enjoyed it.
In the lift, a colleague and I discussed the weather for four floors, then went quiet. When the doors opened, we both said 'Have a good one' and walked opposite ways.
Stuck umbrella
My umbrella flipped inside out in the wind. I walked three streets holding a mangled metal flower and trying to look dignified.
The wind snapped my umbrella the moment I stepped outside. I carried it to the bin like a fallen soldier and went on getting soaked.
Shopping trolley
Trolley with the wobbly wheel again. It's always me. I think it recognises me and goes for the worst one on purpose.
I picked a trolley with a squeaky wheel and spent the whole shop apologising to the aisles.
Doorbell
Doorbell rang, courier dumped a parcel and legged it before I got downstairs. It was for next door. Of course it was.
The doorbell rang twice, and by the time I opened it there was only a parcel and a cloud of exhaust. The label had the wrong flat number, naturally.
Taxi ride
Taxi driver played music so loud the window rattled. He knew every word. By the end I knew a few and tipped him double.
The taxi driver sang along to the radio the whole journey, and I found myself humming too.
Packed lunch
Mum packed jollof and a banana. Everyone at school had crisps. By Friday three people wanted my jollof, so I'd say it worked out.
My mum packed rice and plantain every day and I used to be embarrassed by it. These days I'd give almost anything for one of those lunch boxes.
Old trainers
My trainers have a hole in the toe and one lace is knotted four times. I refuse to retire them. They know me.
My oldest trainers have a split sole and a lace tied in a bow of defeat.
Waiting for the kettle
Kettle takes four minutes to boil. I've learned to use the time to check the post, find a mug, and have a small argument with myself.
Our kettle takes ages to boil, so I tidy the worktop and stare out of the window. It's the closest thing I get to meditation.
Home DIY
Put up a shelf, it was crooked, so I put up a second one at the same angle to look intentional. It now looks like a design choice.
Hung a shelf and it came out slightly off, so I added a second to match the slope. Everyone now thinks I planned it, and I've stopped correcting them.
Cold house
The heating's been off since Tuesday and I'm typing this wearing a hat indoors. The cat has decided my lap is the only warm place.
Our heating packed up and we've been living in layers. The dog sleeps on my feet, and I've started drinking tea purely for the warmth.
Wrong number
Got a wrong-number text from a stranger who's now telling me about their day. I haven't had the heart to correct them.
A stranger texted me by mistake and we've exchanged four messages about their lunch.
Fish and chips
Chips on the seafront, wind trying to steal them, gull watching from the wall with total intent. I lost one chip, defended the rest.
Ate fish and chips on the seafront, guarding the bag from a gull with a very personal interest. It cost me two chips and a little dignity.
Library card
Renewed my library card and the woman at the desk said I hadn't borrowed anything in six years. I was a little ashamed. Borrowed three books.
I renewed my library card after years away and left with five books I'll probably return late. The librarian just smiled and stamped them.
Broken zip
My coat zip died on the coldest day. Walked home holding it shut with one hand and carrying shopping with the other.
The zip gave out on my favourite coat, so I've spent the week holding it closed with a safety pin and some stubbornness.
Sunday cleaning
Cleaning the flat on a Sunday means finding things I lost months ago. Found a tenner, a sock, and the remote. No regrets.
On Sunday I cleaned the flat and found a missing earring, two pens and a receipt from 2022. I felt unreasonably proud.
Public speaking
Gave a talk to forty people. My hands shook so much the slides looked like they had a pulse. Someone said it was fine afterwards.
My first talk in front of the team went fine until a slide wouldn't load. I filled the gap with a joke and, to my surprise, it landed.
Rooftop view
Went up to the roof with a flask of tea. The whole city looked weirdly quiet, like someone had turned down the volume.
From the roof the city looked small and slow, and for once I wasn't in a hurry. I stayed until the tea was cold.
Lost phone
Rang my phone from my partner's, heard it buzzing from inside the sofa. Relief, then a quiet feeling of being an idiot.
I panicked, searched the car, and borrowed a phone to ring mine. It was in my coat pocket the whole time, and I'm leaving that out of the story.
School run
Did the school run in my slippers by accident. Nobody said anything, but one dad nodded at them with what I'd call respect.
I realised halfway to school that I was wearing two different shoes. A mum nodded at me kindly, like it happens to everyone.
Cooking disaster
Tried making pancakes for the family. First one stuck, second burned, third landed on the floor. We had cereal.
I tried a new recipe from a video and it went wrong in several creative ways.
Tea round
In our office the tea round is a political act. If you skip someone, it'll be remembered for months.
At work the tea round has unwritten rules, and everyone knows who's been missed. I'm now very careful about whose mug I overlook.
Raining at the market
The stall holders pulled tarps over everything and carried on, like rain was just another customer. I bought a scarf I didn't need.
It rained the whole morning at the market, but the traders kept shouting prices from under their tarpaulins. I bought plums out of respect.
Neighbour's dog
The neighbour's dog barks at everything, including its own reflection. Last night it barked at a leaf. A single leaf.
The dog next door barks at the postman, the wind and the moon. I've started to like it, as it makes me feel like the street is guarded.
Cinema trip
Went to the cinema, someone behind me explained the film to their friend throughout. I didn't need the commentary but I got it.
The cinema was almost empty, but a man chose the seat directly behind me and ate crisps through the whole film. It was a very loud film too.
Evening walk
Evening walks have become the best part of my day. No phone, just the streetlights coming on and other people's windows glowing.
I started taking an evening walk and now I look forward to it. Nobody needs me, and the windows along the road are like small stories.
Birthday dinner
Booked a restaurant for her birthday, they put 'Happy Anniversary' on the dessert. She ate it anyway and laughed. Good sport.
We celebrated at a small Italian place where the waiter sang loudly and slightly off key. She went red, then asked him to do it again.
Autumn leaves
Walking to work through piles of leaves, kicking them like a kid. A woman gave me a look, then kicked one herself.
The path was thick with leaves and I couldn't resist a few good kicks. A runner went by and grinned, and I felt twelve again.
Quiet morning
The house is quiet in a way I only notice when I'm not in it. The tap drips, the radiator ticks, and a lorry downshifts somewhere far off.
The house holds a particular quiet in the mornings. I hear the tap, the radiator settling, a distant lorry changing gear, and somehow it feels like company.
Old coat
I still wear his coat, though the sleeves are too long. In the pockets I find tissues, a bus ticket, a pen that doesn't work. I don't throw them out.
I wear my father's coat even though it is too big. The pockets still hold a bus ticket, a pen with no ink, and a crumpled tissue, and I leave them there.
Station goodbye
We said goodbye on the platform with our usual small jokes. The train pulled out and I stood there a moment, waving at nobody in particular.
We said goodbye on the platform the way we always do, with a joke. When the train left I kept waving a little too long at the empty track.
New town
In a new town you learn the streets by the people you pass. The man with the dog, the woman with the red door. Slowly it becomes a map.
A new town becomes familiar through repetition: the same man walking the same dog, the same woman on the same step. Gradually you start to belong.
Winter evening
By four it's dark and the windows turn into mirrors. I draw the curtains and the room becomes smaller and kinder.
By four o'clock the dark has arrived and the windows reflect the room back. I close the curtains, and the house seems to draw closer around me.
A borrowed book
The book I borrowed from her still has her pencil marks in the margins. I read it slowly, like a conversation I've been invited into.
The book I borrowed has her pencilled notes in the margins. I read slowly, partly for the story and partly to hear her voice again.
Grandfather's watch
His watch runs four minutes fast. I've never corrected it. Somehow I like arriving early on his time.
My grandfather's watch runs a few minutes ahead, and I have never set it right.
Funeral flowers
The flowers were too bright for the day. A cousin said so quietly, and we both laughed, then stopped, then held onto each other.
The flowers were far too cheerful for the occasion. A cousin whispered it, and we laughed, then went quiet, then reached for each other's hands.
First day of term
The uniform was a size too big, 'to grow into'. I pulled the sleeves over my hands and walked in as if I belonged to the building.
My blazer was a size too large, bought to be grown into. I rolled the sleeves back and walked through the gates, hoping no one would look.
Night bus
The night bus hums like a refrigerator. Everyone on it is tired in a different way, and nobody pretends otherwise.
The night bus hums quietly through the empty streets. Each passenger is tired in their own way, and there is a strange comfort in it.
Handwritten recipe
Her recipe says 'cook until it smells right'. I've made it forty times and I think I'm finally getting close.
Her recipe says to cook it until it smells right. I have made it many times, and only now do I think I understand what she meant.
Bridge at night
The bridge is lit orange and the river underneath is black. I stop halfway, the way everybody does, and look at nothing for a while.
The bridge glows orange above the dark river. Halfway across I stop, like everyone does, and look at the water for no good reason.
Missed call
I saw her name on the missed calls and didn't ring back that night. The next morning it was too late. I keep the phone charged anyway.
Her name appeared among the missed calls and I told myself I would ring tomorrow. I still keep that phone charged, in case it rings.
The long way home
I take the long way home on Fridays, through the park, past the closed café. It adds nine minutes and removes the week.
On Fridays I walk the long way home, through the park and past the shuttered café. It adds ten minutes and takes the week away.
Radio at night
The radio was on low, a man reading out football scores to no one. I fell asleep halfway through Leicester.
I fell asleep to the radio, a quiet voice reading scores to an empty kitchen. By the end it was only a murmur.
Moving out
I left the key on the counter and stood in the doorway longer than I needed to. The room looked smaller without us in it.
I put the key on the kitchen counter and lingered at the door. Without our things, the room seemed to shrink back into itself.
Sea in November
The sea in November is the colour of old pewter. A few dogs, a man with a metal detector, and the wind going right through my coat.
In November the sea turns a flat grey. Only a few dog walkers and a lone man with a metal detector remain, and the wind finds every gap in my coat.
Old friend's house
Her house still smells of toast and lavender polish. I sat in the same chair I used to at fifteen and nobody said a word about it.
Her house smelled of toast and lavender, exactly as I remembered. I sat in my old chair and, for a minute, I was fifteen again.
Letter from home
The envelope had her shaky handwriting and a stamp stuck on crooked. I opened it carefully, to make it last.
The envelope was addressed in her unsteady handwriting, the stamp slightly crooked. I opened it slowly, wanting the moment to last.
The last customer
The cafe was closing and the owner kept the lights on for me. I finished my tea slowly, grateful, and left a bigger tip than I could afford.
The café was shutting, but the owner let me stay and finish my tea. I left too much money on the table and felt only slightly foolish.
